MATCH (company:Company {ticker: $ticker})
MATCH (company)-[:REPORTS]->(fact:FinancialFact)
MATCH (fact)-[:FOR_PERIOD]->(period:FiscalPeriod)

    'SalesRevenueNet'

ORDER BY period.period_year ASC, filing.filing_date DESC

RETURN company.ticker AS ticker,

results.question: What risks did NVIDIA describe in its 2022 10-K?
results.answer:
NVIDIA’s 2022 Form 10‑K identifies several distinct risk categories:
• Market and technology risk – failure to meet evolving market needs, identify new products, or adapt to rapid changes in gaming, data‑center, professional visualization and automotive markets could harm revenue and financial results (evidence_fe0976557dc7671e7dddf021).
• Design‑win risk – lengthy design‑win processes, unanticipated industry‑standard changes, or lack of compliance with standards may prevent revenue generation (evidence_fe0976557dc7671e7dddf021).
• Acquisition risk – difficulties completing acquisitions (e.g., regulatory challenges in the Arm transaction), integration challenges, retention of talent, liability assumptions, financing constraints, and potential dilution or loss of value (evidence_e7c6c38d8dfa900f14687c94, evidence_a83cdb1f35168aa20e6aed26).
• Cyber‑security and data‑protection risk – security breaches, ransomware, supply‑chain attacks, and reliance on third‑party services could disrupt operations, increase expenses, and damage reputation (evidence_7b5956b6a432504f4cd3feb1, evidence_e7c6c38d8dfa900f14687c94).
• COVID‑19 pandemic risk – ongoing disruptions to global supply chains, financial markets, and operational execution, with uncertain impacts on demand and liquidity (evidence_6f178643e471c03425904e09).
• Regulatory, legal and climate‑related risk – complex laws, carbon taxes, fuel/energy taxes, pollution limits, and climate‑related litigation or reputational harm could increase costs and affect product design and demand (evidence_a83cdb1f35168aa20e6aed26).
• General operational and financial volatility – fluctuations in operating results, customer payment issues, environmental liabilities, and changes in accounting standards could affect stock price and financial condition (evidence_6f178643e471c03425904e09).

evidence.text: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS In evaluating NVIDIA, the following risk factors should be considered in addition to the other information in this Annual Report on Form 10-K. Purchasing or owning NVIDIA common stock involves investment risks including, but not limited to, the risks described below. Any one of the following risks could harm our business, financial condition, results of operations or reputation, which could cause our stock price to decline, and you may lose all or a part of your investment. Additional risks, trends and uncertainties not presently known to us or that we currently believe are immaterial may also harm our business, financial condition, results of operations or reputation. Risks Related to Our Industry and Markets If we fail to meet the evolving needs of our markets, or to identify new products, services or technologies, our revenue and financial results may be adversely impacted. Our accelerated computing platforms address four large markets: Gaming, Data Center, Professional Visualization, and Automotive. These markets experience rapid changes in technology, customer requirements, new product introductions and enhancements, and industry standards. Our strategic and business success depends on our ability to: • timely identify emerging industry changes, and develop new or enhance existing products, services and technologies that meet the evolving needs of these markets; • expand the ecosystem for our products and technologies; • accurately forecast demand in our businesses; • meet customer safety and compliance standards, which are subject to change; • manage product, software, and service lifecycles to maintain customer and end user satisfaction; • develop infrastructure needed to scale our business, including related to our acquisitions, customer support, e-commerce and IP licensing capabilities; and • complete technical, financial, compliance, sales and marketing investments for some of the above activities. We make considerable investments in research and development and business offerings in markets where we have a limited operating history, which may not produce meaningful revenue for several years, if at all. If we fail to develop new products, services and technologies, or if they do not become widely adopted, our business, revenue, financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected. Achieving design wins, which is important to our success in several businesses, may involve a lengthy process and depend on our ability to anticipate features and functionality that customers will demand. Unanticipated changes in industry standards or disruptive technological innovation could render our products incompatible with products developed by other companies. If our products are not in compliance with prevailing industry and safety standards, our customers may not incorporate our products into their design strategies. Failure to obtain a particular design win may prevent us from obtaining future design wins in subsequent generations. Furthermore, a design win does not guarantee revenue. We cannot ensure that our strategic direction will result in products and technologies that provide value to our customers and partners. If we fail to anticipate the changing needs of our target markets and emerging technology trends, or if we do not appropriately adapt our strategies as

target operate; • potential failure of our due diligence processes to identify significant issues with the assets or company in which we are investing or are acquiring; and • impairment of relationships with, or loss of our or our target’s employees, vendors and customers, as a result of our acquisition or investment. System security and data protection breaches, as well as cyber-attacks, could disrupt our operations, reduce our expected revenue and increase our expenses, which could adversely affect our stock price and damage our reputation. Security breaches, computer malware, social-engineering attacks, denial-of-service attacks, software bugs, server malfunctions, software or hardware failures, loss of data or other information technology assets, and other cyber-attacks are increasingly sophisticated, making it more difficult to successfully detect, defend against them or implement adequate preventative measures. For example, on February 23, 2022, we became aware of a security incident involving unauthorized access to our network by a group of independent criminal threat actors, not affiliated with any government or political cause. results.question: How have NVIDIA's risks changed over the years?
results.answer: NVIDIA’s risk disclosures have broadened over time. In the 2019 filing the company focused on general market‑related risks such as the need to meet evolving market needs, heavy investment in R&D, and intense competition across its four core segments (gaming, professional visualization, datacenter, automotive)【evidence_417096443da5920ef0061b3a】. By 2021 the filing added more specific operational risks, including the need to accurately forecast demand and scale utilization in the data‑center business, integration of the Mellanox networking acquisition, and compliance with safety standards for automotive solutions【evidence_f6c36da994a334364361b2e1】. The 2023 filing introduced a much larger set of distinct risk categories, covering demand‑supply mismatches, reliance on third‑party suppliers, product defects, macro‑economic and geopolitical exposure, cyber‑security breaches, business disruptions, climate‑change impacts, integration of acquisitions, customer concentration, talent retention, internal‑control disruptions, and COVID‑19 effects【evidence_5c073fa599226552d8a7bf33】. The 2024 filing highlighted emerging uncertainties tied to new product lines and use cases, such as generative AI demand volatility, CPU product demand forecasting, geopolitical tensions affecting Taiwan/China supply chains, and cryptocurrency‑mining demand fluctuations for GPUs【evidence_c5f1576d815b4d7dd9e72576】. The latest 2026 filing added risks related to large‑scale R&D investments in nascent markets, design‑win uncertainties, a significant IP‑license arrangement with Groq, multi‑year cloud‑service agreements, standalone software‑business model execution, and intensified competition, while also reiterating supply‑chain and geopolitical concerns【evidence_e8c1187c4d2ccf7bbe9e37a0】.

results.question: Describe Apple's competitive risks.
results.answer:
Apple faces several competitive risks, including:
- Intense competition from companies with greater technical, marketing, distribution resources and the ability to imitate Apple’s product features, leading to price pressure and reduced margins. (evidence_d61ab66caadc7cb7c606bf38)
- The need to continually introduce innovative products and services; failure to do so or to protect its intellectual property could erode its competitive advantage. (evidence_d61ab66caadc7cb7c606bf38, evidence_21ca5270cc1b611b5a422424)
- Reliance on third‑party intellectual property and components; loss of licenses, infringement claims, or supply disruptions could limit product offerings and increase costs. (evidence_2522a881b8aeb7c3bca06029)
- Dependence on third‑party developers and content providers; reduced support or higher licensing costs could diminish the appeal of Apple’s devices. (evidence_2522a881b8aeb7c3bca06029)
- Competitive pressures in the markets for smartphones, PCs, tablets, and wearables, where Apple holds only a minority share and some markets experience little growth or contraction. (evidence_d61ab66caadc7cb7c606bf38)
- Potential regulatory and legal actions that could force product modifications, limit IP enforcement, or require sharing innovations, harming Apple’s competitive position. (evidence_21ca5270cc1b611b5a422424)

results.question: What risks did Apple describe in its 2024 10-K?
results.answer:
Apple’s 2024 Form 10‑K lists a broad range of risk factors, including:
- Regulatory and legal compliance risks, such as new and changing laws, export/import regulations, ESG reporting expectations, and potential violations that could lead to bans, delays, fines, or reputational harm (evidence_a626068b37169c2fcc7e6550; evidence_e5589c28ed0e7ea5fe49446e).
- Tax risks, including changes in tax rates, new international tax rules, audits by tax authorities, and uncertainty in tax law interpretation that could increase effective tax rates (evidence_d6c1b68cd8c5579a9f0e6eb5).
- Stock price volatility, which may affect share repurchase pricing and investor expectations (evidence_d6c1b68cd8c5579a9f0e6eb5).
- Legal proceedings and intellectual property disputes, particularly patent claims, which can be costly, time‑consuming, and disruptive (evidence_e5589c28ed0e7ea5fe49446e).
- Retail operation risks, including macro‑economic impacts on retail activity, store construction and operating costs, lease renewals, and inventory valuation (evidence_e5589c28ed0e7ea5fe49446e).
- Supply chain and component risks, such as shortages, price volatility, reliance on single‑source or custom components, supplier financial health, and potential delays in component or product shipments (evidence_3f212d7d74de749a0e00c560).
- Product design and manufacturing defect risks that could harm reputation, cause safety issues, or lead to liability (evidence_3f212d7d74de749a0e00c560).
- Market and demand risks, including shifts in product mix, compressed product life cycles, macro‑economic pressures, inflation, foreign‑exchange fluctuations, and dependence on a single major product (evidence_4b45d67179f659a2d1c7c420).
- Currency risk, where foreign‑exchange rate movements affect sales, costs, margins, and the value of derivative hedges (evidence_4b45d67179f659a2d1c7c420).

results.question: What risks does Amazon describe in its 10-K?
results.answer:
Amazon’s 2025 Form 10-K lists a variety of risk factors, including:

- **Payments‑related risks**: reliance on third‑party providers for credit‑card, debit‑card, electronic check and promotional financing services; potential disruption if these providers cease services; exposure to payment‑card association rules, data‑security requirements and possible fraud or breaches that could increase fees, fines or limit the ability to accept payments (evidence_c3d0987aa0f8182502014dab, evidence_1b1e82b304d5f7e0648f2d13).
- **Regulatory and compliance risks**: obligations under payment, money‑laundering, international transfer, privacy, data‑security, data‑localization, consumer‑protection and electronic‑fund‑transfer laws; risk of civil/criminal penalties, fines, or forced cessation of services if violations occur (evidence_c3d0987aa0f8182502014dab, evidence_1b1e82b304d5f7e0648f2d13).
- **Inventory risk**: exposure to seasonality, new product launches, rapid product‑cycle changes, tariffs, defective merchandise, shifts in consumer demand and tastes, spoilage, and lead‑time or prepayment requirements that could lead to overstocking, markdowns or write‑offs (evidence_1b1e82b304d5f7e0648f2d13).
- **Geopolitical and regulatory risk in China and India**: reliance on third‑party licenses, potential changes in regulatory, licensing or trade policies, fines, loss of licenses, or forced restructuring/shutdown of operations in those markets (evidence_cacf9792f64af62dc09532cb).
- **Operational variability and fulfillment/network risk**: fluctuations in demand, seasonal peaks, promotions, product launches, economic conditions, natural or human‑caused disasters, extreme weather, and geopolitical events that can strain fulfillment and data‑center capacity, increase shipping costs, cause service interruptions or require costly inventory management adjustments (evidence_cacf9792f64af62dc09532cb, evidence_0ad9d41ebf8d43afec0ce19b).
- **Regulatory investigations and litigation risk**: ongoing investigations and potential enforcement actions related to competition, consumer‑protection, privacy, data‑use, and other regulations; associated legal costs, potential fines, reputational damage, and operational disruption (evidence_96b82f116c24763bba899099, evidence_0ad9d41ebf8d43afec0ce19b).
- **Litigation and government proceedings risk**: exposure to claims, lawsuits, and regulatory proceedings covering intellectual‑property, taxes, labor, antitrust, privacy, data security, AI services, healthcare, and other matters that could result in legal costs, operational disruption, or adverse financial impacts (evidence_96b82f116c24763bba899099).
- **Stock price volatility and capital‑structure risk**: high volatility of Amazon’s common‑stock price driven by interest‑rate changes, technology trends, quarterly operating results, market conditions, analyst estimates, and potential need to issue additional equity or debt, which could affect profitability and financing availability (evidence_c3d0987aa0f8182502014dab).
- **Climate‑change and environmental risk**: increased operating costs from extreme weather events, higher investment needs for a low‑carbon transition, potential demand reductions, greater compliance costs, and reputational damage (evidence_0ad9d41ebf8d43afec0ce19b).

results.question: What risks does Meta describe in its 10-K?
results.answer:
Meta identifies a broad set of risk factors in its 2025 Form 10‑K, including:
- Risks related to product offerings, such as the ability to add and retain users, maintain user engagement, retain marketer spending, availability of data signals for ad targeting, operating effectively with mobile operating systems and partners, and the success of new or existing products (evidence_3e88e03b605df9e5018ce0ba).
- Risks related to business operations and financial results, including competitive pressures, fluctuations in financial results, adverse media coverage, challenges in building, maintaining, and scaling technical infrastructure, disruptions to service, operating in multiple countries, litigation (including class actions), and integrating acquisitions (evidence_3e88e03b605df9e5018ce0ba).
- Risks related to government regulation and enforcement, covering government restrictions on access to Meta’s products, complex and evolving U.S. and foreign privacy, data‑use, content moderation, competition, youth safety, consumer protection, advertising, and other laws (e.g., GDPR, DMA, DSA, UK OSA, EU AI Act, DMCC), and the impact of investigations, enforcement actions, and settlements (evidence_3e88e03b605df9e5018ce0ba).
- Risks related to data, security, platform integrity, and intellectual property, including security breaches, cyber‑attacks, hacking, phishing, malware, false user accounts, and attempts to misuse the platform, which could harm reputation, cause service interruptions, and result in financial loss (evidence_df2abd8d49e1398600aa9d70).
- Risks related to ownership of Class A common stock, such as volatility in the stock price driven by fluctuations in revenue, analyst expectations, secondary stock sales, investor sentiment, competitive announcements, user‑base changes, broader market conditions, index inclusion/exclusion, media coverage, litigation, and regulatory actions (evidence_1b59af4edeaadb6271375db3).
- Risks of negative publicity and media coverage, especially concerning misinformation, illicit use of products, geopolitical events, elections, and ongoing litigation, which could reduce user engagement and advertiser demand (evidence_21c07bfaff58ee0a3f0326a8).
- Risks of catastrophic events and crises, such as pandemics, natural disasters, terrorism, geopolitical conflict, power loss, and cyber‑attacks, which can affect user base, product development, supply chains, financial markets, and capital access (evidence_21c07bfaff58ee0a3f0326a8).
- Risks associated with significant operating expenses and investments, particularly in artificial intelligence initiatives and Reality Labs, which may reduce operating margin and profitability if not successful (evidence_21c07bfaff58ee0a3f0326a8).
- Risks related to AI development and deployment, including potential legal liability, uncertain market acceptance, and possible adverse impacts on business, reputation, and financial results (evidence_c7461c600f0b59284ff351a9).
- Risks from product and investment decisions that may reduce short‑term financial results, such as changes to user‑data practices, ad‑targeting capabilities, feed algorithms, ad size/frequency, and the introduction of new features that could shift user engagement away from higher‑monetizing products (evidence_c7461c600f0b59284ff351a9).

results.question: What risks does Microsoft describe in its 10-K?
results.answer:
Microsoft’s 10‑K identifies a range of risk categories, including:
- Strategic and competitive risks, such as intense competition, low barriers to entry, and the need to continuously innovate (evidence_7f2cbe2fc4484ea9ffa50578).
- Risks related to the development, deployment, and use of artificial intelligence, including model flaws, biased data, harmful outputs, regulatory scrutiny, and potential reputational or legal harm (evidence_9a29fa948a442a2ffa1084b3).
- Operational risks tied to expanding infrastructure and capacity demands for its cloud and services platforms (evidence_9a29fa948a442a2ffa1084b3).
- Catastrophic events and geopolitical conditions that could disrupt operations, supply chains, or markets, including earthquakes, cyber‑attacks, terrorist activity, war, and sanctions (evidence_67bc8aadb0a373c4eff267f0).
- Pandemic‑related risks that could affect business, financial condition, and results of operations (evidence_67bc8aadb0a373c4eff267f0).
- Climate‑change and environmental regulatory risks that may impact costs and availability of resources (evidence_67bc8aadb0a373c4eff267f0).
- Security and cybersecurity risks, encompassing threats to Microsoft’s products, services, and customer data, vulnerability exploitation, and potential impacts from AI‑generated code (evidence_91e1fc2d21caa9dc001e3169).
- Risks from reliance on third parties and acquisitions, including limited control over partners, integration challenges, and potential goodwill or intangible impairments (evidence_30e614c63ccec4c6e4176ca2).
- Legal and regulatory challenges related to transactions, acquisitions, and broader compliance, which could adversely affect business and financial results (evidence_30e614c63ccec4c6e4176ca2).
- Platform‑abuse and related security risks, such as misuse of Microsoft’s services and potential liabilities (evidence_30e614c63ccec4c6e4176ca2).

results.question: Describe Amazon's business.
results.answer: Amazon operates as a global, customer‑centric company organized into three primary segments – North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS). It serves a wide range of customers including consumers, sellers, developers, enterprises, content creators, advertisers, and employees. The consumer segment offers online and physical retail stores, a vast selection of products, low prices, fast and free delivery, and subscription services like Amazon Prime. Amazon also designs, manufactures, and sells electronic devices such as Kindle, Fire tablets, Echo, Ring, Blink and eero, and produces media content. For sellers, Amazon provides platforms that enable third‑party merchants to list and fulfill products, earning fees and commissions. Through AWS, Amazon delivers on‑demand cloud computing, storage, database, analytics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning services to developers and enterprises of all sizes. It also supports content creators via publishing and distribution programs, and offers advertising services to sellers, vendors, publishers, and other partners. The company’s operations are supported by extensive fulfillment networks, digital delivery, physical stores, and global customer service centers.

results.question: Describe Alphabet's business.
results.answer: Alphabet Inc. is a collection of businesses led by Google, which it reports in two primary segments—Google Services and Google Cloud—while all other non‑Google businesses are grouped under "Other Bets." Google Services includes Search, YouTube, consumer subscriptions (e.g., YouTube TV, YouTube Music, Google One), the Google Play platform, and hardware such as Pixel devices. Google Cloud provides infrastructure, platform, application, and other cloud services, including AI‑optimized infrastructure, a developer platform (Vertex AI), cybersecurity solutions, data and analytics tools, and AI agents like Gemini Enterprise and Gemini for Google Workspace. Other Bets comprise independent companies at various development stages, ranging from research projects (e.g., X, the moonshot factory) to commercial operations (e.g., Waymo autonomous transportation), generating revenue from autonomous transportation and internet services. The company emphasizes AI as a core, "AI‑first" focus, investing heavily in research and development to build advanced, safe, and responsible AI across its full‑stack approach.

results.question: Describe Meta's business.
results.answer: Meta Platforms, Inc. builds technology that enables people to connect and share across a range of devices and platforms, including mobile phones, personal computers, virtual reality headsets, and AI glasses. Its portfolio, described as the "Family of Apps," includes Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, WhatsApp, Threads, and Meta AI, which provide social networking, photo and video sharing, messaging, and content discovery services. Meta also develops immersive experiences through its Reality Labs division, offering VR products such as Meta Quest devices and related software, as well as AI glasses (Ray‑Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, and prototype AR glasses). The company’s mission is to build the future of human connection and the technology that makes it possible, leveraging artificial‑intelligence investments to power content ranking, advertising tools, generative AI experiences, and product development.

results.question: Describe Microsoft's business.
results.answer: Microsoft operates three reportable segments – Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing – that together deliver a broad portfolio of software, services, devices and content. The Productivity and Business Processes segment includes Microsoft 365 (commercial and consumer) cloud and on‑premises products, LinkedIn’s talent, marketing, premium and sales solutions, and Dynamics 365 applications. The Intelligent Cloud segment (described elsewhere in the filing) provides cloud‑based AI, software, platforms and content services. The More Personal Computing segment covers operating systems, server applications, developer tools, desktop and server management tools, video games, and hardware such as PCs, tablets, gaming consoles and other intelligent devices. Across all segments Microsoft emphasizes AI‑driven productivity, security, compliance, and integrated cloud solutions, and it seeks growth by expanding its installed base, increasing average revenue per user, and shifting customers from on‑premises licenses to cloud subscriptions. The company also highlights its commitment to sustainability, regulatory compliance, and responsible AI development.

results.question: Describe NVIDIA's business.
results.answer: NVIDIA is a data‑center‑scale AI infrastructure company that builds a full‑stack accelerated computing platform. Its business combines hardware (GPUs, CPUs, DPUs, interconnects, networking adapters, and automotive compute modules) with extensive software (the CUDA development platform, CUDA‑X libraries, AI models, training data sets, APIs, SDKs, and domain‑specific frameworks) and services. The company serves four large markets – Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive – offering products such as data‑center GPUs and systems, the Blackwell and Rubin architectures, AI Enterprise and vGPU software licenses, GeForce RTX GPUs for gaming and cloud gaming (GeForce NOW), RTX PRO GPUs for professional design and content creation, and the DRIVE Hyperion platform for autonomous‑driving solutions. NVIDIA’s platform strategy leverages a unified programmable architecture to address diverse workloads, from AI model training and inference to scientific computing, robotics, and 3D graphics, and it is supported by a broad ecosystem of developers and partners.

results.question: Describe Apple's business.
results.answer:
Apple Inc. designs, manufactures and markets a broad portfolio of consumer electronics, software and services. Its hardware includes iPhone smartphones (e.g., iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 16), Mac computers (MacBook Air/Pro, iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro), iPad tablets (iPad Pro, iPad Air, iPad, iPad mini), wearables (Apple Watch Series 11, Apple Watch SE 3, Apple Watch Ultra 3), AirPods and Beats audio products, and the Apple Vision Pro spatial computer. The company also offers home devices such as Apple TV 4K, HomePod and HomePod mini, and a range of accessories.  

Its services span advertising, AppleCare support, cloud storage, and digital content platforms (App Store, Apple Arcade, Apple Fitness+, Apple Music, Apple News+, Apple TV). Payment services include Apple Card and Apple Pay.  

Apple organizes its operations geographically—Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific—and sells products directly through its retail and online stores and via indirect channels (cellular carriers, resellers). In 2025, direct and indirect channels accounted for roughly 40% and 60% of net sales, respectively.  

The business is highly competitive, facing aggressive price pressure, rapid product cycles, and the need for continual innovation across hardware, software and services. Apple relies on a mix of internally developed technology and licensed third‑party intellectual property, and must manage component supply constraints and licensing arrangements to sustain its product pipeline.

results.answer: Microsoft's revenue grew from $245.122 billion in fiscal 2024 to $331.839 billion in fiscal 2026, an increase of $86.717 billion, or 35.377% year‑over‑year. results.question: Describe Apple's business in its 2018 10-K.
results.answer: Apple’s 2018 Form 10‑K describes a diversified consumer‑technology business that designs, manufactures and markets a range of hardware, software and services. Its hardware portfolio includes iPhone smartphones, iPad tablets, Mac computers, Apple Watch smartwatches, Apple TV set‑top boxes and accessories such as AirPods, Beats products, HomePod and iPod touch. The company develops operating systems for each platform—iOS, macOS, watchOS and tvOS—and offers a suite of services, including the iTunes Store, App Store, Apple Music, iCloud, Apple TV App Store, Apple Book Store and other digital content and subscription services. Apple sells directly to consumers and small‑ and mid‑sized businesses through its retail stores, online store and direct sales force, and also uses indirect channels such as carriers, wholesalers, retailers and resellers, which together accounted for 71% of net sales in 2018. The firm emphasizes ongoing investment in research and development, marketing and advertising, and leverages a large developer ecosystem and third‑party accessories to enhance its integrated hardware‑software‑services offerings. No single customer contributed more than 10% of net sales, and the company faces intense competition across all product and service categories.

results.question: Describe Amazon's business in its 2019 10-K.
results.answer: Amazon.com, Inc. operates as a diversified global commerce and technology company organized into three operating segments: North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS). The company serves a wide range of primary customer groups—consumers, sellers, developers, enterprises, and content creators—through its online and physical retail stores, subscription services (such as Amazon Prime), advertising programs, and a broad portfolio of electronic devices (e.g., Kindle, Fire tablets, Echo). It provides a marketplace platform that enables third‑party sellers to list and sell products, earning fees based on sales, per‑unit activity, or interest. Amazon also offers cloud computing, storage, and related services to developers and enterprises via AWS, and supports content creators through Kindle Direct Publishing and other media publishing programs. The business emphasizes selection, low price, and convenience, including fast and reliable fulfillment through its North American and International fulfillment networks, co‑sourced and outsourced arrangements, digital delivery, and physical stores. Seasonal factors drive higher sales in the fourth quarter, which historically accounts for about one‑third of annual revenue. The company employs roughly 798,000 full‑time and part‑time workers (as of December 31 2019) and utilizes independent contractors and temporary staff. Intellectual property, including trademarks, patents, and copyrights, is regarded as critical to its success.

results.question: Describe Alphabet's business in its 2020 10-K.
results.answer: Alphabet operates as a collection of businesses organized into two primary segments: Google Services and Google Cloud, with all remaining non‑Google businesses reported as "Other Bets." Google Services includes its core search engine, advertising platforms, YouTube, and other consumer products such as Google Assistant. Google Cloud generates revenue from fees for Google Cloud Platform services and Google Workspace collaboration tools. "Other Bets" comprises earlier‑stage businesses and emerging technologies, some of which generate revenue while others are in research, development, or early commercialization stages. Competition is broad, spanning general‑purpose search engines, vertical search and e‑commerce sites, social networks, digital advertising platforms, cloud providers, and consumer hardware manufacturers.

results.question: Describe Meta's business in its 2021 10-K.
results.answer: Meta Platforms, Inc. describes its business as a company that builds technology and products to help people connect, build community, and bring the world closer together, including through immersive experiences for the metaverse. Its offerings are organized into two primary segments: (1) Family of Apps (FoA), which generates virtually all revenue from advertising placed on its platforms—Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, WhatsApp, and related services—and (2) Reality Labs (RL), which generates revenue from sales of consumer hardware, software, and content such as Meta Quest virtual‑reality headsets and Facebook Portal devices. Meta’s products enable users to share moments, discover content, communicate via text, audio, and video, and engage in commerce across mobile devices, personal computers, VR/AR headsets, wearables, and in‑home devices. The company reports a global workforce of 71,970 employees as of December 31 2021 and operates from its headquarters in Menlo Park, California, with offices in more than 80 cities worldwide. It emphasizes an inclusive workplace, diversity initiatives, and remote‑work options, and notes its transition toward immersive AR/VR experiences as part of its metaverse strategy.

results.answer: Microsoft describes itself as a technology company whose mission is to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. It operates three reportable segments: (1) Productivity and Business Processes – providing Office (commercial and consumer), Microsoft Teams, LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365 solutions; (2) Intelligent Cloud – delivering cloud infrastructure and platform services; and (3) More Personal Computing – encompassing Windows, Surface devices, gaming, and related services. Microsoft also underscores its commitment to diversity, inclusion, and human capital development, noting that it employs approximately 221,000 full‑time employees globally as of June 30, 2022, and that it leverages employee feedback through surveys to shape its culture and programs.

results.question: Describe NVIDIA's business in its 2023 10-K.
results.answer: NVIDIA operates two primary segments: Compute & Networking, which includes its data‑center accelerated computing platform, networking, automotive AI cockpit and autonomous‑driving solutions, electric‑vehicle computing platforms, Jetson robotics, NVIDIA AI Enterprise software, and cryptocurrency mining processors; and Graphics, which comprises GeForce GPUs for gaming and PCs, the GeForce NOW streaming service, Quadro/NVIDIA RTX GPUs for enterprise workstations, virtual GPU software, automotive infotainment platforms, and Omniverse Enterprise software for metaverse and 3D‑internet applications. The company serves four large markets—Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive—providing GPUs, DPUs, interconnects, software, SDKs, and services that accelerate AI, data analytics, graphics, and scientific computing workloads. Key product lines include the GeForce RTX 40 Series gaming GPUs (based on the Ada Lovelace architecture) and the NVIDIA RTX platform for professional visualization and real‑time ray tracing. NVIDIA also offers the CUDA programming model, which enables general‑purpose GPU computing for high‑performance computing (HPC) applications across aerospace, bio‑science, energy, and other fields. Additionally, NVIDIA’s automotive segment delivers AI‑driven solutions for autonomous vehicles and infotainment under the DRIVE Hyperion brand, and its Omniverse platform supports virtual world simulation and collaboration for 3D workflows. The company reported a $1.35 billion acquisition termination cost in fiscal year 2023 due to the aborted acquisition of Arm Limited, and it had 26,196 employees worldwide at fiscal‑year end.

results.question: What risks did Amazon describe in its 2018 10-K?
results.answer:
Amazon’s 2018 Form 10‑K identified a wide range of risk factors, including:
• Significant inventory risk – exposure to seasonality, new product launches, rapid product‑cycle changes, pricing, defective merchandise, consumer demand shifts, spoilage and the difficulty of forecasting demand for new products (evidence_c88e90356307d4501f90f407, evidence_533cd03e0a771af3a2776a37).
• Intellectual property risks – challenges protecting trademarks, patents, trade secrets and domain names, potential infringement claims, and the need for substantial resources to enforce rights (evidence_c88e90356307d4501f90f407).
• Product liability and insurance coverage – possible insufficient liability insurance and lack of indemnification in vendor agreements (evidence_09184ba863dcf7b5b67e54ac).
• Payments‑related risks – exposure to regulatory changes, fraud, interchange fee increases, reliance on third‑party payment processors, compliance with card‑association rules, and potential loss of payment‑processing capabilities (evidence_09184ba863dcf7b5b67e54ac).
• Data loss and security breaches – risk of loss or misuse of large volumes of data, breaches of vendor or customer systems, and insufficient security despite protective measures (evidence_533cd03e0a771af3a2776a37).
• System interruption and lack of redundancy – occasional website or service outages, potential damage from natural disasters, terrorism, cyber‑attacks, and insufficient disaster‑recovery planning (evidence_533cd03e0a771af3a2776a37).
• International operational risks – economic and political conditions, regulatory and trade barriers, currency restrictions, limited infrastructure, longer receivable cycles, privacy and data‑protection laws, staffing challenges, and geopolitical events (evidence_4c70730f428a3b760ed9d29d).
• Intense competition – numerous competitors across physical retail, e‑commerce, digital content, cloud services, logistics, with some having greater resources, brand recognition, or more aggressive pricing (evidence_3a830739c9e7012ca97e54f6).
• Strain from rapid expansion – complexity and resource pressure from scaling global operations, new products, services, technologies, and geographic regions, potentially harming reputation and operating results (evidence_3a830739c9e7012ca97e54f6).
• Fluctuations in operating results and growth – difficulty forecasting growth, high fixed expenses, and limited ability to adjust spending quickly (evidence_3a830739c9e7012ca97e54f6).

results.question: What risks did Alphabet describe in its 2019 10-K?
results.answer:
Alphabet identified a variety of risk factors in its 2019 Form 10‑K, including:

• Intellectual property risks – potential infringement claims, inadequate indemnities from suppliers, and the difficulty of protecting patents, trademarks, trade secrets and copyrights, which could harm its products, services, brand value and competitive position. (evidence_48d846ebcd5fba36f8a9d15a, evidence_005824895d6aae3ca84d7299)
• Stock‑repurchase and ownership concentration risks – uncertainty around share‑repurchase programs, potential volatility in the stock price, and the concentration of voting power in Larry Page and Sergey Brin that limits other shareholders’ influence. (evidence_48d846ebcd5fba36f8a9d15a)
• Advertising‑related risks – heavy reliance on advertising revenue, exposure to reduced advertiser spending, loss of partners, ad‑blocking technologies, changes in advertising policies, and macro‑economic conditions that could lower ad demand. (evidence_0659db75c2378bd856d91edb)
• Competitive and innovation risks – intense competition across multiple markets, the need to continually innovate, and the risk that Alphabet may fail to deliver useful products and services, which could erode its market position. (evidence_0659db75c2378bd856d91edb)
• Margin‑pressure risks – expansion into new businesses (hardware, Google Cloud, Google Play, gaming, subscription products, Other Bets) that may have lower margins, as well as increased costs from competition, partner agreements, infrastructure, and promotion of new products. (evidence_005824895d6aae3ca84d7299)
• Security, privacy and data‑breach risks – bugs, theft, misuse, vulnerabilities, cyber‑attacks, and potential failures in security controls that could lead to loss or disclosure of proprietary or user information, legal exposure, reputational damage and harm to the business. (evidence_31f403b743792d0117211b69)
• Market‑related risks – volatility and extreme price fluctuations in the broader stock market and technology sector, which can affect the market price of Alphabet’s Class A and Class C shares regardless of operating performance. (evidence_42f60b2ecf67ff00e82eae85)
• Analyst and earnings‑expectation risks – potential negative impact from analyst recommendations, earnings announcements that differ from expectations, and the lack of earnings guidance. (evidence_42f60b2ecf67ff00e82eae85)

results.question: What risks did Meta describe in its 2020 10-K?
results.answer:
Meta’s 2020 Form 10‑K Item 1A identifies a broad set of risk factors, including:
- Risks related to product offerings, such as the ability to add and retain users, user engagement, loss of marketer spending, reduced data signals for ad targeting, mobile operating system changes, and the performance of new or existing products (evidence_fa6d0b6553825ff54f72e632, evidence_7c7e712a27447411e64d09d3).
- Risks related to business operations and financial results, including the impact of the COVID‑19 pandemic, competitive pressures, volatile or slower user and revenue growth, integration of acquisitions, scaling technical infrastructure, service disruptions, operating in multiple countries, and litigation (evidence_fa6d0b6553825ff54f72e632, evidence_75bcb7d10e27d55bcc65c30b).
- Risks related to government regulation and enforcement, such as government restrictions on access to Meta’s products, evolving privacy, data‑use, content, competition, consumer‑protection laws, investigations and enforcement actions, and compliance with regulatory privacy requirements, including a consent order with the FTC (evidence_fa6d0b6553825ff54f72e632, evidence_7c7e712a27447411e64d09d3).
- Risks related to data, security, and intellectual property, including security breaches, improper access or disclosure of data, cyber incidents, and the ability to obtain, maintain, protect, and enforce intellectual property rights (evidence_7c7e712a27447411e64d09d3).
- Risks related to ownership of Class A common stock, such as volatility in the stock price and limitations on shareholder influence due to the dual‑class structure (evidence_75bcb7d10e27d55bcc65c30b).
- Risks related to international operations and supply chain, covering compliance with anti‑corruption, export‑control, and sanctions laws, design/manufacturing/supply‑chain challenges for consumer hardware, quality issues, reliance on third‑party manufacturers and logistics providers, pandemic‑related disruptions, macro‑economic or geopolitical events, and inventory risk (evidence_47a508d6092eb7ec744c9550, evidence_66d8d21df4b8e71896ba558b).

results.question: What risks did Apple describe in its 2022 10-K?
results.answer:
Apple’s 2022 Form 10‑K lists a wide range of risk factors, including:
- Economic downturns and credit/collectibility risks, limited ability to issue debt, reduced liquidity and declines in the fair value of financial instruments (evidence_f09b9562baf24a248fd009ee).
- Impacts of the COVID‑19 pandemic, such as supply chain disruptions, reduced consumer demand, operational interruptions and heightened other risks (evidence_f09b9562baf24a248fd009ee; evidence_3f70c6093f2ce6bed3096d15).
- High‑cost retail store investments, lease commitments, and potential lease termination, equipment write‑offs, and severance costs if stores underperform or close (evidence_a638cce53d6b7da4bad3f5bf).
- Legal and regulatory risks, including ongoing and increasing patent claims, litigation, government investigations, and potential indemnification obligations (evidence_a638cce53d6b7da4bad3f5bf).
- Political, trade, and international dispute uncertainties that could affect consumer confidence, spending, and operations (evidence_3f70c6093f2ce6bed3096d15).
- Natural disasters, earthquakes, industrial accidents, fire, power shortages, nuclear accidents, terrorist attacks, and other business‑interrupting events (evidence_3f70c6093f2ce6bed3096d15).
- Climate‑change‑related increases in frequency/intensity of natural disasters that could disrupt manufacturing, supply chains and service delivery (evidence_3f70c6093f2ce6bed3096d15).
- Reliance on single or limited sources for critical components, creating heightened vulnerability to supply interruptions (evidence_3f70c6093f2ce6bed3096d15).
- Cybersecurity threats, including ransomware, malicious attacks, unauthorized access to confidential information, and associated reputational, legal and financial impacts (evidence_80ae555a14da35d5bb4b2e10).
- Compliance and regulatory risks across many areas (anti‑corruption, import/export, foreign exchange, AML, tax, environmental, health, safety, e‑waste, climate change), which can increase costs, limit product offerings, create uncertainty, and expose Apple to penalties or reputational harm (evidence_096e6264b872bca5dbb4bba0).

results.question: What market risks did NVIDIA describe in its 2024 10-K?
results.answer:
In its 2024 Form 10‑K, NVIDIA described two primary market risks:

1. **Interest rate risk** – Exposure related to the company’s fixed‑rate investment portfolio and its outstanding senior notes. A parallel shift of ±0.5% in the yield curve would change the fair value of the investments by $93 million, while the senior notes are carried at face value and are not subject to interest‑rate‑related fair‑value changes because they bear a fixed rate. 
2. **Foreign‑exchange rate risk** – Although the company’s sales are in U.S. dollars and it uses forward contracts to hedge, fluctuations in the U.S. dollar could affect competitiveness and supplier costs. A 10% strengthening of the U.S. dollar would have lowered accumulated other comprehensive income (loss) by $116 million (2024) and $112 million (2023), and an adverse 10% foreign‑exchange movement would have reduced income before taxes by $60 million (2024) and $36 million (2023).

results.question: How has Microsoft's business evolved over the years?
results.answer: Microsoft’s business has expanded and shifted focus over time while retaining its core of software, services, and devices. In 2019 the filing described a broad portfolio that included operating systems, productivity applications, server software, development tools, video games, and hardware such as PCs, tablets, and gaming consoles, together with cloud‑based services, consulting and online advertising (evidence_6f8c9ff2537d47f3f2d28e85). By 2021 the company highlighted its leadership team and emphasized its cloud and enterprise strategy, reflecting a growing emphasis on cloud services and enterprise solutions (evidence_63ff4f1852353d328d870606). The 2023 filing underscored a deepening investment in artificial intelligence across the entire suite of products—Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Bing, Xbox—and the integration of generative AI (“copilot”) into consumer and commercial cloud offerings, while still describing the same range of software, devices, and advertising services (evidence_80339f34785697d7c8fad338). The 2024 filing reiterated AI as a central pillar, detailing AI‑powered features such as Microsoft 365 Copilot, role‑specific Copilot for Sales, Service and Finance, and the broader AI‑first positioning of Microsoft 365, while continuing to reference its traditional products and services (evidence_058d74502cb07234e1118c5e). The 2026 filing presented a future‑oriented view, grouping the business into three operating segments—Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing— and highlighting new strategic themes such as end‑to‑end security solutions, AI‑driven workplace transformation, cloud‑based ubiquitous computing, frontier AI capabilities, AI training programs, and innovations in gaming and Windows‑enabled cloud services (evidence_ddc623e571c669d7ae395ece). Overall, Microsoft has evolved from a diversified software‑and‑hardware company to a cloud‑centric, AI‑focused enterprise that organizes its operations around productivity, intelligent cloud, and personal computing segments.

results.question: How has Apple's business evolved over the years?
results.answer: Apple’s business has broadened and deepened its product and services portfolio over time. In 2018 the company described its core offerings as mobile communication and media devices (iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, AirPods, Apple TV, HomePod) together with a suite of software, operating systems and digital content services such as iTunes, App Store and iCloud, sold worldwide through retail, online and third‑party channels【evidence_5efec2163e65823867e61736】. By 2020 the filing emphasized the expansion of digital content platforms and subscription services—including Apple Arcade, Apple Music, Apple News+, Apple TV+ and the newly announced Apple Fitness+—as well as payment services like Apple Card and Apple Pay, while noting that sales were split roughly 34% direct and 66% indirect and that no single customer contributed more than 10% of net sales【evidence_1bc87c2862e24213e5d72bf6】. The 2022 filing listed a more extensive hardware lineup (iPhone 14 Pro, iPhone 14, iPhone 13, iPhone SE, MacBook Air/Pro, iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro, iPad Pro/Air/mini, Apple Watch Ultra, Apple Watch Series 8, Apple Watch SE, AirPods Pro/Max, Beats, HomePod mini) and highlighted services such as advertising, AppleCare, cloud services, digital content platforms, and payment services【evidence_c3c973ca712d46765c78eaa3】. The 2023 filing continued this trend, adding the iPhone 15 series, Apple Watch Ultra 2, Apple Watch Series 9, and expanding the Home and Accessories categories (Apple TV, HomePod, HomePod mini) while maintaining the same suite of services (advertising, AppleCare, cloud, digital content subscriptions, payment services)【evidence_70c4885f88d548bf28307c72】. The most recent 2025 filing shows further diversification with new product categories such as the spatial computer Apple Vision Pro and the “Apple Watch Series 11, Watch SE 3, Watch Ultra 3,” while retaining the full range of existing devices and services, indicating a continued strategy of integrating hardware, software, and subscription‑based services across an expanding ecosystem【evidence_29ad174ccbc0a6133a4a6a32】.

MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS The following Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations (“MD&A”) is intended to help the reader understand the results of operations and financial condition of Microsoft Corporation. MD&A is provided as a supplement to, and should be read in conjunction with, our consolidated financial statements and the accompanying Notes to Financial Statements (Part II, Item 8 of this Form 10-K). This section generally discusses the results of our operations for the year ended June 30, 2026 compared to the year ended June 30, 2025. For a discussion of the year ended June 30, 2025 compared to the year ended June 30, 2024, please refer to Part II, Item 7, “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” in our Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended June 30, 2025. OVERVIEW Microsoft is a technology company committed to making digital technology and artificial intelligence (“AI”) available broadly and doing so responsibly, with a mission to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. We create platforms and applications, powered by AI, that deliver innovative solutions that meet the evolving needs of our customers. results.question: What market risks does Apple describe?
results.answer: Apple describes exposure to two market risks: (1) Interest rate risk – fluctuations in U.S. interest rates that can affect the fair value of its investment portfolio and increase interest expense on term debt; and (2) Foreign exchange rate risk – changes in currency exchange rates, especially a stronger U.S. dollar, that can reduce net sales, gross margins, and affect the fair values of assets and liabilities.

judgment.reason: The answer accurately lists the two market risks (interest rate risk and foreign exchange rate risk) described in Apple's Item 7A Market Risk section for fiscal year 2025, and it is fully supported by the provided evidence.

evidence.text: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk The Company is exposed to economic risk from interest rates and foreign exchange rates. The Company uses various strategies to manage these risks; however, they may still impact the Company’s consolidated financial statements. Interest Rate Risk The Company is primarily exposed to fluctuations in U.S. interest rates and their impact on the Company’s investment portfolio and term debt. Increases in interest rates will negatively affect the fair value of the Company’s investment portfolio and increase the interest expense on the Company’s term debt. To protect against interest rate risk, the Company may use derivative instruments, offset interest rate–sensitive assets and liabilities, or control duration of the investment and term debt portfolios. The following table sets forth potential impacts on the Company’s investment portfolio and term debt, including the effects of any associated derivatives, that would result from a hypothetical increase in relevant interest rates as of September 27, 2025 and September 28, 2024 (dollars in millions): Interest Rate Sensitive Instrument Hypothetical Interest Rate Increase Potential Impact 2025 2024 Investment portfolio 100 basis points, all tenors Decline in fair value $ 2,416 $ 2,755 Term debt 100 basis points, all tenors Increase in annual interest expense $ 129 $ 139 Foreign Exchange Rate Risk The Company’s exposure to foreign exchange rate risk relates primarily to the Company being a net receiver of currencies other than the U.S. dollar. Changes in exchange rates, and in particular a strengthening of the U.S. dollar, will negatively affect the Company’s net sales and gross margins as expressed in U.S. dollars. Fluctuations in exchange rates may also affect the fair values of certain of the Company’s assets and liabilities. To protect against foreign exchange rate risk, the Company may use derivative instruments, offset exposures, or adjust local currency pricing of its products and services. However, the Company may choose to not hedge certain foreign currency exposures for a variety of reasons, including accounting considerations or prohibitive cost. The VAR model used a Monte Carlo simulation. Based on the results of the model, the Company estimates, with 95% confidence, a maximum one-day loss in fair value of $590 million and $538 million as of September 27, 2025 and September 28, 2024, respectively. results.question: Summarize Apple's latest MD&A discussion.
results.answer:
Apple’s Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) for fiscal 2025 covers several key topics.  
- **Product, service, and software announcements** – The company introduced new hardware throughout the year (e.g., MacBook Pro, Mac mini, iMac, iPad mini in Q1; iPhone 16e, iPad Air, MacBook Air, Mac Studio in Q2; iOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26, iPadOS 26, watchOS 26, visionOS 26, tvOS 26 in Q3; iPhone 17 series, Apple Watch Series 11, AirPods Pro 3 in Q4)【evidence_08eeca0fdb7c191c31e27b90】.

Gross margin rose to $195.2 billion (46.9 % of sales) with product margin slightly down (36.8 %) and services margin up (75.4 %). Operating expenses increased 8 % to $62.2 billion, reflecting higher R&D and SG&A spend, primarily from headcount and variable selling costs【evidence_28ef6ad78ddb2a22bd4d2276】【evidence_e5de537b1eb9c123654da3ea】.  
- **Liquidity and capital resources** – Apple held $132.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities and expects this, together with cash flow and debt market access, to meet its cash needs and capital return program.  Contractual obligations include $91.3 billion of fixed‑rate notes (with $12.4 billion due within 12 months), $8.0 billion of commercial paper, $16.8 billion of lease payments, $56.2 billion of manufacturing purchase obligations, $14.8 billion of other purchase obligations, and $8.8 billion of deemed repatriation tax payable【evidence_44e88cae38f12866c0227537】【evidence_e5de537b1eb9c123654da3ea】.  
- **Tax considerations** – The effective tax rate fell to 15.6 % in 2025, lower than the statutory 21 % due to foreign earnings, R&D credits, share‑based compensation benefits, and other factors, resulting in a $10.7 billion reduction in the provision for income taxes versus 2024【evidence_e5de537b1eb9c123654da3ea】.  
- **Risks and uncertainties** – The MD&A notes exposure to macroeconomic conditions (inflation, interest rates, currency fluctuations), U.S. and foreign tariffs that could affect supply chains and pricing, and uncertainties around tax positions and legal proceedings, all of which could materially impact results【evidence_08eeca0fdb7c191c31e27b90】【evidence_594a91ce45e6718160ffe1a4】.

results.question: Summarize Amazon's latest MD&A discussion.
results.answer: Amazon’s Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) emphasizes several key points.  It outlines the company’s primary revenue sources—product sales (including third‑party seller items) and service sales such as AWS, advertising, Prime subscriptions, and digital content—while focusing on long‑term, sustainable free cash flow growth driven by operating income and efficient management of working capital and capital expenditures (evidence_cb0481f70ff885d22d348364).  The company reports that 2025 net sales grew 12% year‑over‑year to $716.9 billion, with North America sales up 10%, International sales up 13%, and AWS sales up 20%; foreign‑exchange effects added $4.4 billion to sales (evidence_2c3c20a46bcab6ea5a4307b7).  Operating income guidance for Q1 2026 is $16.5‑$21.5 billion, reflecting higher AI‑related costs, quick‑commerce investments, and pricing pressures (evidence_32e22a73f380b8996317814e).  The MD&A highlights significant investments in technology and infrastructure—including AI, a satellite broadband network, and autonomous‑vehicle initiatives—that support both Amazon’s retail operations and AWS, with 2025 technology costs rising due to infrastructure spending and foreign‑exchange impacts (evidence_fcba8e6efa09fb5c3f32a848).  Fulfillment costs increased in 2025, driven by higher sales volume and network expansion, though offset by operational efficiencies (evidence_c26b95d004ce5fe3acafbe87).  The discussion also lists a broad set of forward‑looking risks, such as foreign‑exchange fluctuations, energy prices, global economic and geopolitical conditions, supply‑chain volatility, competition, and the outcomes of ongoing litigation and regulatory investigations (evidence_cb0481f70ff885d22d348364).

results.question: Summarize Alphabet's latest MD&A discussion.
results.answer:
Alphabet’s Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) for 2025 focuses on several key themes:

* **Growth drivers and AI integration** – The company highlights long‑term trends such as expanded AI offerings in Search, Google Cloud, and other products, expecting AI‑driven user engagement to boost revenues, though it notes increasing competition could affect growth rates and margins (evidence_c60d06a3a5aae7aae5e8f40b).
* **Revenue mix shift** – Revenues from cloud, consumer subscriptions, platforms and devices are growing faster than advertising, becoming a larger share of total revenue, but with generally lower margins than advertising (evidence_c60d06a3a5aae7aae5e8f40b).
* **Cost structure** – Cost of revenues rose $16.2 billion to $162.5 billion, driven by higher TAC and other costs, but the cost‑of‑revenues percentage fell to 40 % (evidence_a1933981b45a89da379efe41, evidence_cae3c98b2d9f1f69ce0f33d7). Research and development expenses increased $11.8 billion to $61.1 billion, mainly from employee compensation and depreciation (evidence_a1933981b45a89da379efe41). General and administrative costs rose $7.3 billion due to legal matters, including a $3.5 billion EU fine (evidence_a1933981b45a89da379efe41).
* **Segment performance** – Google Services operating income grew $18.1 billion to $139.4 billion; Google Cloud income rose $7.8 billion to $13.9 billion; Other Bets loss widened to $7.5 billion, largely from Waymo compensation (evidence_e6f63472913edc5c08e3713b).
* **Revenue growth** – Total revenues increased $52.8 billion to $402.8 billion, driven by strong growth in Google Search & other (+$26.4 billion), YouTube ads (+$4.2 billion), Google subscriptions/platforms/devices (+$7.7 billion), and Google Cloud (+$15.5 billion) (evidence_5594a58fd4efa7491ea6e2e8, evidence_cae3c98b2d9f1f69ce0f33d7).
* **Cash flow and investments** – Operating cash flow was $164.7 billion; capital expenditures $91.4 billion, mainly for technical infrastructure. The company issued $37.3 billion of senior notes and repurchased $45.4 billion of stock (evidence_5594a58fd4efa7491ea6e2e8).

results.question: Summarize Microsoft's latest MD&A discussion.
results.answer: Microsoft’s MD&A for fiscal year 2026 highlights strong growth in its cloud and subscription businesses and ongoing investments in AI. Revenue rose 18% to $331.8 billion, driven by a 27% increase in Microsoft Cloud revenue to $214.4 billion and a 84% jump in commercial remaining performance obligations to $678 billion. Segment revenues grew: Productivity and Business Processes up 16% ($140.0 billion), Intelligent Cloud up 30% ($137.8 billion), while More Personal Computing was flat to slightly down. Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue grew 17% and Consumer cloud revenue 28%; Azure and other cloud services rose 41%; LinkedIn revenue increased 11%; Dynamics 365 grew 18%; Windows OEM and Devices declined slightly, and Xbox content/services fell 5%. Gross margin improved 16% to $225.5 billion, though the Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage slipped to 66% due to AI infrastructure spending. Operating expenses rose 7% to $70.2 billion, reflecting higher R&D, AI talent, and Copilot advertising costs. Net income increased 31% to $133.7 billion, with diluted EPS up 32% to $17.95, partially boosted by gains from OpenAI investments. The filing notes that foreign‑currency effects added roughly 2% to revenue and operating income, and it emphasizes ongoing AI initiatives, a strategic partnership with OpenAI, and the importance of its commercial metrics for tracking performance. Seasonality and global economic factors, including trade restrictions and currency fluctuations, remain risk considerations.

results.question: Summarize NVIDIA's latest MD&A discussion.
results.answer: NVIDIA describes itself as a data‑center‑scale AI infrastructure company that has expanded from PC graphics into compute, networking, and AI‑driven applications.  In fiscal 2026, revenue growth was driven by its Compute & Networking segment, especially data‑center compute and networking platforms built on the Blackwell architecture, with Data Center compute revenue up 59% and networking revenue up 142% (evidence_805ff1a4909740244d098a4f).  The company began shipping its new Blackwell Ultra platforms (including GB300) in Q2 FY2026, but acknowledges that product transitions and complex system configurations can cause production delays, supply‑demand challenges, inventory volatility, quality issues, higher material costs, and warranty expenses (evidence_f1305ee3b31a0a03e4c4c791).  A $4.5 billion charge for H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations in Q1 FY2026 reduced gross margins from 75.0% to 71.1% (evidence_6eda7875766a35deacfb4ca4).  NVIDIA also notes external constraints such as limited data‑center energy capacity, capital availability for customers, and export licensing requirements for its H20 product to China, which could affect future revenue (evidence_f1305ee3b31a0a03e4c4c791).  Revenue is concentrated among a few direct and indirect customers—one direct customer accounted for 22% of FY2026 revenue and another for 14%, while some indirect customers represent 10% or more each (evidence_6eda7875766a35deacfb4ca4).  International sales remain significant, representing 31% of FY2026 revenue (evidence_6eda7875766a35deacfb4ca4).  The MD&A also discusses revenue recognition practices, including sales return allowances, customer program accruals, and the handling of contracts with multiple performance obligations (evidence_94205246972c8c5550665fa9).  Finally, the filing highlights ongoing tax considerations, deferred tax asset assessments, and non‑marketable equity securities measured at cost less impairment (evidence_0011c05eef98db8450207646).

Since our original focus on PC graphics, we have expanded to several other large and important computationally intensive fields. results.question: How has Amazon's business evolved over the years?
results.answer: Amazon’s business has expanded and become more diversified over time. In 2018, Amazon described its operations as encompassing fulfillment and delivery networks, physical stores, digital delivery, and a range of seller programs that generate fees, as well as AWS services for developers and enterprises, and publishing services for authors and content creators (evidence_aed14788b51554f284c936b9). By 2020, the filing emphasized continued competition and highlighted the importance of its intellectual property portfolio, while noting that seasonality affects sales and that its workforce had grown to about 1.3 million employees (evidence_abbdf0948eb740a21a102af5). The 2022 filing reiterated the competitive pressures, detailed ongoing investment in technology, infrastructure, fulfillment and marketing, and reported further growth in staff to roughly 1.54 million employees (evidence_0f29a3014f6b72130e982ac4). In the 2023 filing, Amazon continued to stress competition, the role of intellectual property, seasonality, and an even larger workforce of about 1.525 million employees, along with expanded safety and talent‑development programs (evidence_abd0414d961a6ee4ebef5865). The most recent 2025 filing notes that the business remains subject to rapid change and new competitors, continues to invest heavily in technology, infrastructure, fulfillment and marketing, and reports a workforce of approximately 1.576 million employees (evidence_d19ee40860eb105a6f402b91). Across these filings, Amazon’s evolution is marked by a broadened product and service portfolio, sustained growth in employee headcount, increasing emphasis on technology and logistics capabilities, and ongoing competitive and intellectual‑property challenges.

results.question: How has Alphabet's business evolved over the years?
results.answer: Alphabet’s business has evolved from a single internet search company into a diversified collection of businesses organized under the Alphabet holding structure. Early filings describe the founders’ intent to be “unconventional” and to make “smaller bets” beyond core search, leading to the creation of non‑Google businesses that are now reported as “Other Bets” (e.g., self‑driving cars, life sciences, internet access, TV services)【evidence_48004d8f5777ff8aba80c6dc】. Over time the company formalized its segment reporting: Google is now split into Google Services and Google Cloud, while all remaining ventures remain in Other Bets【evidence_0298508ea975730872447700】【evidence_03e8b1e982507f2cf307dac3】【evidence_37b3529e30c1eb6f8d6b94c0】. The business narrative consistently highlights a shift from purely helping users find answers to enabling them to “get things done,” expanding into AI‑first products, large‑scale cloud services, and a suite of consumer platforms such as YouTube, Google Assistant, and Google Pay【evidence_03e8b1e982507f2cf307dac3】【evidence_37b3529e30c1eb6f8d6b94c0】. Investment in research and development has grown dramatically, from over $100 billion in the prior five years to more than $200 billion by the 2025 filing, reflecting the company’s deepening focus on AI, machine learning, and advanced infrastructure【evidence_03e8b1e982507f2cf307dac3】【evidence_ca7adf681047d0bafde3a6ac】. Overall, Alphabet has progressed from a search‑centric firm to a multi‑segment, AI‑driven technology conglomerate that balances mature Google Services with high‑risk, high‑reward Other Bets.

results.question: How have Microsoft's risks changed over the years?
results.answer:
Microsoft’s risk disclosures show a broadening and deepening of concerns over time. In 2019 the company highlighted emerging AI‑related reputational and liability risks, operational outages, and quality or supply problems with hardware and software. By 2021, the focus expanded to the increasing cost and complexity of building and maintaining datacenter infrastructure, risks of data loss or connectivity failures, and heightened dependence on sole‑source suppliers for components. In 2023 the filing added new operational risks tied to the transition to clean energy, environmental regulations, and geopolitical disruptions affecting datacenter land, power, and GPU availability, while still emphasizing AI‑driven challenges and infrastructure demands. The 2024 filing introduced supply‑chain disruption risks for hardware assembled in Asia and emphasized legal and regulatory scrutiny, especially antitrust enforcement and competition law actions in multiple jurisdictions. The most recent 2026 filing further amplified AI‑related risks, noting potential flaws in AI models, biased data, harmful content, regulatory and ethical issues, and the need for human oversight, alongside continued concerns about infrastructure capacity and supply constraints.

Overall, Microsoft’s risk profile has evolved from primarily operational and product‑quality concerns with an early mention of AI, to increasingly detailed infrastructure, supply‑chain, regulatory, and AI governance risks, reflecting the growing scale of its cloud, AI, and hardware businesses.

Management said the performance was driven primarily by growth in advertising revenue, which was boosted by higher ad impressions delivered (up 12% year‑over‑year) and an increase in average price per ad (up 9% year‑over‑year). The online commerce vertical was the largest contributor to the advertising revenue increase, and other revenue grew 50% due to paid messaging from WhatsApp and Meta Verified subscriptions. Reality Labs revenue also rose modestly, helped by sales of AI glasses.

judgment.reason: The answer provides the total revenue figure of $200.97 billion for 2025, which matches the graph evidence. It also correctly summarizes management's statements from the MD&A about advertising growth driven by higher ad impressions (+12%) and higher price per ad (+9%), the online commerce vertical as the largest contributor, other revenue growth from paid messaging and Meta Verified, and modest Reality Labs revenue increase due to AI glasses. All statements are supported by the supplied evidence.

results.question: What was Amazon operating income in 2025 and explain what management said drove performance?
results.answer: Amazon reported operating income of $79,975 million for the year ended December 31, 2025. Management said the performance was driven primarily by increased unit sales and advertising sales across its North America and International segments, and by higher sales in AWS, which were partially offset by higher fulfillment, technology, infrastructure, shipping, and other operating costs. The increase in North America operating income reflected strong unit and advertising sales, while International operating income grew due to similar sales drivers. results.question: How did Apple's revenue change from 2024 to 2025 and explain what management said drove the trend?
results.answer: Apple's revenue increased by $25.126 billion, or 6.426 %, from $391.035 billion in fiscal 2024 to $416.161 billion in fiscal 2025. **AI infrastructure‑related risk themes**

- **Amazon (AMZN)** – Rapid global expansion and the adoption of artificial‑intelligence and machine‑learning technologies increase the complexity and scale of Amazon’s infrastructure. The company warns that this growth can place significant strain on its management, operational, financial and internal control resources, and that failure to manage that growth could damage its reputation and operating results【evidence_1faa19c74237ee09d6861208】.

- **Alphabet (GOOGL)** – Alphabet notes that the development and deployment of AI‑driven features may create new security vulnerabilities. AI‑centric attacks could exacerbate cyber‑security risks, including breaches and phishing attempts that target its systems, employees or users【evidence_4d846f077451489ec48810cd】.

- **Meta (META)** – Meta highlights a broad set of AI‑related infrastructure risks, including the need for substantial investment in AI compute and talent, and exposure to harmful or illegal content, misinformation, bias, intellectual‑property infringement, data‑privacy and cybersecurity issues. The company also faces uncertain regulatory treatment of AI‑generated content and the risk that AI‑driven features may not deliver the expected efficiency or profitability【evidence_e63c53b81cf64938acc2660b】.

- **Microsoft (MSFT)** – Microsoft identifies several AI infrastructure risks: flawed AI algorithms, biased or insufficient training data, and ethical concerns that could lead to reputational harm or legal liability. Additionally, the scaling of AI services places heavy demands on its data‑center and network infrastructure, raising the risk of outages, data loss, and operational disruptions【evidence_13f28cc0e13e7b094befd894】【evidence_2d490d593bccd741f9147f70】.

results.question: Compare the businesses described by Apple, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta in their 2025 10-K filings.
results.answer:
Apple describes its business as focusing on creating an open, collaborative work environment where managers and team members can contribute, grow and succeed, with an emphasis on employee safety, security and inclusion. The company provides information to investors through its SEC filings and corporate websites, and references that its reports are available free of charge on investor.apple.com (evidence_c9a7596eda76c75ae41b51aa).

Amazon outlines a business model centered on customer obsession, offering a wide selection of products at low prices with fast delivery across its three operating segments: North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS). It serves consumers, sellers, developers, enterprises, content creators and advertisers, and highlights its extensive fulfillment network, physical stores, and subscription services such as Amazon Prime (evidence_d19ee40860eb105a6f402b91; evidence_053a3dee59ab4c8aa4230bc0).

Alphabet (Google) emphasizes the importance of complying with a complex, evolving global regulatory environment that can affect its cost of doing business, product offerings and competitive position. The company relies on intellectual property—including trademarks, copyrights, patents and trade secrets—to protect its technology and brand, and notes that further information on these matters is included in its risk factors and legal disclosures (evidence_5bfbb7b5df81e6e85c3316e9).

Meta describes its corporate structure, incorporation details and branding, noting that its trademarks and service marks such as Meta, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and others are owned by Meta Platforms, Inc. The company provides its annual reports and other SEC filings on its investor website and uses its corporate and social media channels to disclose material information to investors (evidence_a08c2b7855799ee0a9f03034).

The company may use derivatives, offsetting, or duration control to mitigate these risks. [evidence_d2ca178b6f8b97544386d29e]

**Amazon (AMZN)** – Amazon reports *foreign exchange risk* tied to its International segment (23% of revenue), where fluctuations can materially affect net sales and operating results, and it quantifies potential losses on foreign‑denominated cash, cash equivalents, marketable securities, and intercompany balances under adverse exchange‑rate scenarios. The filing also mentions *equity investment risk* related to market price volatility of its equity, warrant, and convertible debt holdings. [evidence_3a741943888ed875df233098]

**Alphabet (GOOGL)** – Alphabet identifies *interest rate risk* affecting the fair value of its investment portfolio (VaR analysis) and notes that its senior unsecured notes are fixed‑rate, so interest‑rate fluctuations generally do not impact consolidated statements, though the notes’ fair value will change with market rates. It also highlights *equity investment risk* (market price volatility of both marketable and non‑marketable equity securities) and provides a hypothetical 10% price decline impact. [evidence_6b8565b34c925444175cbcf2]

**Meta (META)** – Meta’s filing lists three market‑risk categories: *foreign currency exchange risk* (revenue and expenses denominated in non‑USD currencies, especially euros, with a stronger USD potentially reducing revenue and operating results), *interest rate risk* (impact on interest income and market value of cash equivalents, marketable debt securities, and long‑term debt, with a 100‑basis‑point rate rise reducing the market value of available‑for‑sale securities), and *equity price risk* (fair‑value volatility of marketable and non‑marketable equity investments, with a hypothetical 10% price drop decreasing fair value). [evidence_033ef6b5e71c91ff726295c5] [evidence_72f53b9881beb3551457dadf]
